# On the Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

I've been thinking lately about how rarely we get properly lost anymore. Not in the metaphorical sense—though God knows there's plenty of that going around—but the honest, geographical kind where you take a wrong turn and end up somewhere you didn't intend to be.

My phone knows exactly where I am at all times. It knows where I'm going. It knows seventeen different routes to get there, ranked by efficiency. It knows which of those routes has the best coffee shops if I want to make a detour. It has essentially eliminated one of humanity's oldest forms of mild adventure, and I'm not sure we've adequately mourned this loss.

I remember the last time I was genuinely, unmistakably lost. It was maybe five years ago in a small town in Portugal that I can't quite remember the name of. My phone had died—fully, completely dead in that way phones used to die before we all carried portable battery packs like anxious talismans. I had a general sense that my hotel was "that way," which in navigational terms means absolutely nothing. So I started walking.

What followed was two hours of wandering through narrow streets that twisted back on themselves in what felt like a deliberately mischievous pattern. I passed the same bakery three times. A woman watering her plants on a balcony started to recognize me by my increasingly confused expression. But instead of feeling frustrated, I felt something I can only describe as liberated. There were no notifications pinging at me. No sense of time wasted. No awareness of how many steps I'd taken or calories I'd burned. There was just me, the cobblestones, the smell of salt from the nearby ocean, and the genuine uncertainty about what was around the next corner.

I eventually found my hotel (it was closer than I thought), but what I took from that experience was more interesting than the destination itself. It was the memory of what it felt like to be genuinely surprised by geography. To turn a corner and think, "Oh, I've never seen this before," without immediately knowing its Yelp rating or whether it was historically significant.

This connects to something I've been puzzling over: our relationship with optimization. We've spent the last twenty years systematically removing friction from daily life, and it's been largely wonderful. I'm not romanticizing the pre-internet era—I remember it, and there was plenty to complain about. Waiting on hold with a customer service representative for forty-five minutes now seems like a relic of a barbaric age. Truly, technology has made much of life better.

But I wonder if in optimizing for efficiency, we've accidentally optimized away some of the things that make being alive interesting. The best moments in my life have almost always been inefficient ones. They involved detours, distractions, unexpected conversations, or simply being in the wrong place at the right time. These things can't be scheduled. They can't be optimized for. They require a certain amount of slack in the system, a willingness to not be heading toward something specific.

I've started noticing this in how we consume media, too. I used to browse a bookshelf at random and discover books. I'd flip through a magazine at a doctor's office and find an article I would never have searched for intentionally. Television had commercials that forced you to see advertisements for products you didn't know existed. These were inefficiencies, but they were also how serendipity worked.

Now the algorithm shows me things it thinks I'll like based on things I already like. This makes logical sense—it's what I asked for, in a way. But it creates a funhouse mirror effect where we end up only encountering variations on ourselves. My recommendations are increasingly tailored to me, which means they're increasingly less likely to surprise me.

There's a particular kind of joy in being surprised. Not shocked or frightened, but surprised—delighted by encountering something you didn't know you wanted to encounter. When was the last time you stumbled onto a song, book, or idea completely by accident? Not through algorithmic suggestion, but through actual happenstance?

I think about this a lot because I recognize I'm not immune to this trend. I've been optimizing my own life gradually, without really noticing it. My calendar is color-coded. I have a carefully curated morning routine. I've eliminated "wasted time" from my day. And while these things are efficient and productive, I've also noticed that I'm less creative, less surprising to myself. I know what I'm thinking before I think it, because my thoughts have been well-organized into efficient neural pathways that go exactly where they're supposed to go.

So I've started doing something small: once a week, I try to do something inefficiently. I'll take a different route somewhere and actually observe my surroundings. I'll browse a physical bookstore without a list. I'll start a conversation with someone without knowing where it's going. Nothing dramatic. Just small rebellions against optimized living.

These moments feel almost subversive in their ordinariness. I'll be sitting on a bench, having wandered somewhere for no particular reason, and I'll feel something like contentment that my phone didn't suggest I feel. I'll read a book that wasn't recommended to me by any algorithm, and the experience will feel fresher somehow, because it came from pure chance.

I don't think the answer is to abandon technology or efficiency. We can't really go back, and much of what technology provides is genuinely valuable. But I think we need to be more intentional about preserving space for the inefficient, the unexpected, the genuinely lost.

Because here's what I think we've forgotten: being lost isn't actually the worst outcome. Sometimes it's exactly where you need to be.
